title: Wheel Printing
strapline: Toy cars dipped in paint and driven across paper — every wheel leaves a different track.
intent: Children explore transport through creative art rather than only through talk.
Comparing the tracks different wheels leave builds real observational noticing.
Rolling a car across paper is a satisfying whole-arm movement that builds control.
Repeating tracks across a page is early pattern-making.
Children make genuine creative choices about colour, vehicle and direction.
implementation: Provide toy vehicles with visibly different wheels and treads — smooth, chunky, thin, wide.
Set out shallow trays of paint deep enough to coat a wheel but not drown the car.
Use long paper — lining paper or a roll — so children can drive a proper distance.
Model dipping and rolling once, then let children experiment with speed and pressure.
Introduce the vocabulary as they work: tracks, wheels, roll, spin, straight, curved.
Encourage descriptive talk about which wheel made which mark.
Have a bowl of water and a brush so children can clean a car and change colour.
key_questions: Which wheel made that track? How can you tell?
What happens if you roll it fast, or very slowly?
Can you make your car go in a curve instead of a straight line?
Which track is the widest? Which is the thinnest?
What would happen if we used a vehicle with no wheels?

impact.text: Children make choices about colours, materials and tools and mix to see what happens.
Children notice, copy and continue patterns in the tracks they make.
Children match and sort tracks, noticing same and different.
Children use tools with intent and develop an effective grip and control.
Children take up and use new descriptive vocabulary about movement.
Children talk about their own creation and notice detail in others' work.

enhancements: A giant outdoor version with ride-on bikes and trikes through paint trays.
A matching game — match the track back to the vehicle that made it.
Mud, water or chalk tracks outdoors for a non-paint version.
A ramp so children can compare tracks made rolling downhill.
A road-map background printed on the paper for the cars to drive along.
A tyre-print investigation using real bike tyres and a wet patio.

playing_exploring: Children experiment freely with vehicles, paint and speed.
There is no right picture to end up with — the mark is the point.
active_learning: Children repeat and refine a track until it does what they wanted.
They stay at a long roll of paper for a sustained stretch.
creating_thinking: Children predict which wheel will make which mark and test it.
They connect the pattern on the tyre to the pattern on the page.
